title: Model Supply Chain Risk
summary: Model supply chain risk is the exposure created by the origin, packaging, storage and delivery of machine learning models and their associated artefacts. A model is not merely a data file: it is a collection of weight tensors, serialised code, configuration, tokenisers and dependency metadata, and many common storage formats reconstruct objects when loaded, so unpacking an untrusted model can execute attacker supplied code on the loading host. Beyond code execution, the supply chain carries tampering of published weights, poisoning of training or fine tuning data, backdoors that trigger only on specific inputs, typosquatted packages and dependency confusion in the frameworks and adapters a model pulls in. Provenance is the hard part. There is no equivalent of a reproducible build for behaviour, and the artefact is opaque, so a model that performs correctly on a benchmark can still behave differently on a rare trigger, which makes casual testing weak evidence of integrity. Practical control combines documented lineage for every artefact, formats that do not execute code at load time, integrity verification such as signatures or hashes against a trusted source, isolated loading environments with restricted egress, static inspection of artefact contents and dependencies, adversarial evaluation before promotion, and a promotion path that treats a downloaded model like any other third party binary.

beginner.definition: A model is the file that a computer uses after it learns from data, and it lets the computer make predictions or write text. The model supply chain is every step that brings that file to you, from whoever trained it to the website you downloaded it from. Model supply chain risk is the chance that something harmful travels along those steps. The word supply chain means the chain of suppliers involved in making a product.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many teams download a ready made model from a public website and load it the same day. Some model formats run code while they are being opened, so opening the file can already be dangerous. Other files are honest but quietly altered, and they behave strangely on rare inputs you never test. A model can also make mistakes that leak private data. Checking where it came from is as important as testing what it does.
howItWorks: A provider trains a model on data, then publishes the weights and extra files for others to download.
You download the model plus supporting code, settings and libraries it depends on.
Your system loads the file, and some formats rebuild objects, which can run code at that moment.
You test the model on sample inputs before putting it into a real product.
An attacker may tamper with the weights or add a trigger that changes behaviour on one special input.
Defences include checking hashes, using safe file formats, isolating the loading host and reviewing the source.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital that buys a second hand scanning machine from a dealer nobody has used before. The machine looks clean, the manual is glossy and it works perfectly on the first ten patients. But on one rare combination of settings it gives a wrong result, and no one notices for months. A careful hospital asks who owned the machine, checks its service history against the original maker, tests it on many kinds of patient, and runs it in a side room before trusting it. They also lock the machine's network connection so it cannot call home to strangers.
takeaways: Treat a downloaded model like a third party program, not like a harmless document.
Know where the model came from and verify its integrity before loading it.
Load untrusted models in an isolated place, and test behaviour beyond normal examples.

objectives: Explain what the model supply chain covers, from training data and weights to packaging and delivery.
Describe why certain model file formats can execute code when they are loaded.
Identify risks including weight tampering, data poisoning, hidden triggers and dependency confusion.
Explain why provenance and integrity verification are difficult but essential for model artefacts.
List defensive practices such as safe formats, isolated loading, artefact inspection and adversarial testing.
